decisions.quote: Our study attempts to replicate this finding with a much larger data set and more modern statistical methods, but finds it does not hold up: social roles predicted to be associated with adherence to prescriptive language ideologies do not condition the rate of joined variant use for particle verbs in our data.
decisions.reason: The study collects and analyzes a new sample of 10,521 particle verb tokens from the RadioTalk Corpus to re-test Kroch and Small's (1978) published finding, making it a replication. The row was unmatched only because the shipped original metadata was mis-resolved.

decisions.quote: This study shows that Kroch and Small’s finding – that social roles (in radio talk show contexts) condition the rate of joined variant use for particle verbs – does not replicate.

decisions.reason: Once the target identity of row 289 is resolved to Kroch and Small (1978), the authors state an explicit overall verdict in the title, abstract, introduction, and conclusion that the tested social-role effect fails to replicate.

decisions.quote: The English particle verb alternation has been argued to be sensitive to the social role occupied by speakers on radio broadcasts; Kroch and Small (1978) argue that radio show hosts and in-studio guests’ greater sensitivity to prescriptive norms makes them more likely to use the joined variant of the alternation than listeners calling in to the show. This study analyzes 10,521 tokens of variable particle verbs from the RadioTalk Corpus (Beeferman et al. 2019) to try to replicate the effect of speaker role.
decisions.reason: Blind target 0 (Kroch and Small 1978) is not an omitted target; it corresponds to shipped row 289, which was unmatched solely due to a wrong-original metadata resolution error on row 289.
